tier_reason: The ClickBench benchmark_url holds only Velox/Axiom timings. Set against ClickHouse's own ClickBench files, Velox is about 1.7x slower overall, so the ClickHouse claim fails; in any case the compiler is not named and no CPU model is stated, so it could not be A. The re-pointed evidence is the peer-reviewed VLDB 2022 Velox paper (Table 2 and the Figure 4 text): Prestissimo (Presto running on Velox) against Presto Java, with no public benchmark code, compiler or CPU model, so B.

corrections.baseline: Presto Java execution engine (stock Presto vs Prestissimo, i.e. Presto with Velox C++ workers)
corrections.claimed_speedup: VLDB 2022 Table 2, 3TB TPC-H, Prestissimo (Velox) vs Presto Java wall time: Q1 5s vs 42s (8.4x), Q6 1s vs 9s (9x), Q13 15s vs 31s (2x), Q19 6s vs 13s (2.1x); CPU time 6.5x / 3.7x / 2.1x / 2.5x. Replay of production interactive-analytics traffic on two identical clusters: average speedup about 6-7x, with many queries above 10x. Prestissimo also served the same shadowed production workload with 3x fewer servers.
corrections.workload: TPC-H at 3TB (ORC, no zstd compression, lineitem/orders co-partitioned), hand-written query formulations, selected queries Q1, Q6 (CPU-bound) and Q13, Q19 (shuffle/IO-heavy), warm local cache; plus a replay of Meta production interactive-analytics traffic on two clusters with identical hardware
corrections.hardware: 80-node cluster, each node with 64GB RAM and 2x2TB SSD; CPU model not stated in the paper
corrections.caveats: The original ClickHouse claim does not hold. On ClickBench (c6a.xlarge, hits Parquet queried in place through Meta's Axiom SQL CLI; https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/blob/main/velox/results/20260831/c6a.xlarge.json), the sum of best-of-3 times is 214.09s for Velox/Axiom against 124.35s for ClickHouse MergeTree (clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.xlarge.json). Velox wins only 4 of 43 queries (0-based numbering): Q32 10.67s vs 24.23s (2.27x), Q18 12.18s vs 21.84s (1.79x), Q33 10.49s vs 17.57s (1.67x) and Q34 11.13s vs 17.06s (1.53x). It is more than 100x slower on Q0, Q1 and Q19. Against the same-format entry, ClickHouse (Parquet, single) on 2026-09-26, the totals are 214.09s vs 123.75s: Velox wins 5 of 43 queries by 1.08-1.95x, loses 37, and is about 100x slower on Q29 (18.85s vs 0.187s). All of these figures are derived from page data. The 'dishonest academic paper' remark is in ClickBench's velox/README.md, not the top-level README. The paper's numbers are first-party Meta results for a distributed Presto deployment, so the benchmark code is not public and no compiler or CPU model is given. Presto Java is not in the wave's baseline list.

notes: The record's own baseline claim (faster than ClickHouse on ClickBench) fails: Velox is slower in aggregate against both ClickHouse MergeTree and ClickHouse-on-Parquet, and the record also misattributed the 2.3x to Q33 (it is Q32; Q33 is 1.67x). I kept it as a downgrade by re-pointing it to the peer-reviewed VLDB 2022 comparison against Presto Java. If the orchestrator requires a list baseline, reject it as not-faster. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 4,217 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not a fork.

tier_reason: This is NVIDIA's own run of the public duckdblabs/db-benchmark suite, patched to use cudf.pandas (the diff is documented at docs.nvidia.com/cudf/latest/cudf_pandas/benchmarks/). cudf.pandas is not part of the official DuckDB Labs suite or results, which have no cudf solution, so these are first-party numbers on a third-party harness. Hardware and versions are stated but no build details are, so C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Headline 'nearly 150x' (body: 'up to 150x faster', 'minutes to 1 or 2 seconds'). Figure 1 on 5GB: Join takes 4 min 27 s with pandas on CPU vs 1 s with cudf.pandas, and Groupby Advanced 4 min 34 s vs 2 s (~267x and ~137x, derived from page data with GPU times rounded to whole seconds)
corrections.hardware: Blog Figure 1 states 'HW: NVIDIA Grace Hopper, CPU: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480C' (the GH200 SKU is not named); SW pandas v2.2, RAPIDS cuDF 23.10. The linked RAPIDS per-query results (run 2023-11-06, data.rapids.ai/duckdb-benchmark) are labelled 'CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8480CL, GPU: NVIDIA H100'
corrections.caveats: The benchmark was run and published by NVIDIA (the vendor) on the public H2O.ai/DuckDB db-benchmark harness, and cudf.pandas is not in the official DuckDB Labs results. The hardware is asymmetric: a data-center GPU (Grace Hopper per the blog, H100 per the per-query charts) against pandas on a Xeon Platinum 8480C/8480CL, with pandas executing these operations largely single-threaded, and no cost or power normalization is given. The blog says some operations fall back to the CPU. Figure 1's CPU totals (4m27s, 4m34s) do not match the per-query charts, which sum to about 169s for join and about 140s for groupby-advanced. On those per-query charts, cudf.pandas takes 1.31s/0.57s (join) and about 2.85s/2.80s (groupby-advanced) over runs 1 and 2, which is about 129-293x and about 50x over pandas. DuckDB on the same CPU takes 6.17s/4.71s and 7.27s/6.58s, so the GPU gain over a multithreaded CPU engine is only about 2-8x (all derived from page data). Compiler/build flags are not stated.

notes: The 150x headline and the minutes-to-seconds figures are on the page, but the evidence is vendor-run on its own GPU hardware, so C. The record's 'GH200' is not stated (the blog says Grace Hopper) and the per-query results page says H100, a discrepancy. rapidsai/cudf now redirects to NVIDIA/cudf (Apache-2.0, 9,764 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, not a fork); consider updating repo_url.

tier_reason: The README performance chart (docs/super-sirius-perf.png) is first-party and shows every cited time, speedup and cost ratio for Sirius against DuckDB v1.5.5 on TPC-H SF100-SF1000. The TPC-H harness is public (test/tpch_performance/), but no compiler or flags are stated and the per-SF instance and run configuration are not given, so not A. There is no paper or independent suite behind these TPC-H numbers, so C.

corrections.hardware: Sirius (GPU): best of AWS g7e.2xlarge/4xlarge/8xlarge per scale factor (which size won at each SF is not stated), NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark read from a README chart PNG (docs/super-sirius-perf.png); there is no raw results table, and no compiler/build flags are stated. These are hot runs only, and the Sirius time is the best of three g7e instance sizes. The hardware is asymmetric: an RTX PRO 6000 96GB GPU instance against a Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge CPU instance. The chart partly normalizes for this by reporting cost per run (Sirius 2.1-5.3x cheaper). The speedup shrinks from 5.5x at SF100 to 2.7x at SF1000. The page gives no reason, so the earlier explanation (GPU memory/bandwidth bottleneck) is speculation.

notes: Every number in the record matches the chart. I changed last_commit from pushed_at to the default-branch commit date and removed the unsupported bottleneck explanation. The independent ClickBench suite also has Sirius entries: sirius/results/20260309/p5.4xlarge.json has a hot-run sum of 1.50s, against DuckDB at 11.29s (c8g.metal-48xl) and 17.32s (c6a.metal) in the 2026-05-11 runs. That comparison is cross-hardware (GPU vs CPU) and across dates, all derived; re-pointed to it, the record could support tier B.
